description:
Fans of all ages are welcome, costumes encouraged! 

*Registration Required* - It's Free!

Important Event Information:

  • Doors open at 5:45 PM - Available seats will be given to those in the standby line beginning at 6:25 PM

  • Limit of 2 books per person (one personalized, one signature only)
  • Enter the Brandon Mull Universe - Come dressed as your favorite character and you could win our Best Costume Prize!

Signing Line Information: 

  • When you arrive, you'll be assigned a signing group based on your arrival time. 
  • After the presentation, groups will be called one at a time to join the signing line. 
  • If there is a large crowd, the line may take a while - thank you for your patience!

title: Teen Lock-In
description:
Additional Details

  • Thursday, June 25th from 8:00 PM - 11:00 PM in the Library Ballroom and adult Reference areas for ages 12-18 only.
  • No adults will be allowed entry (aside from Library staff and approved volunteers registered to help with this event).
  • There will be games, crafts, a service project (Stuffed Animal Sleepover), and a whole lot of fun!
  • Teens are encouraged to bring snacks and drinks. The Library will provide some snacks as well.
  • The building will be locked at 9:00 PM for the safety of both staff and participating teens. Teens will not be allowed to leave the Library between 9:00 PM - 11:00 PM.
  • The doors on the North side of the Library (facing 600 North) will be unlocked at 11:00 PM. Teens can be picked up at those doors.
  • ALL teens must complete online registration to attend the Lock-In. Registration closes 30 minutes before the event starts.
     

If registration fills up, teens are welcome to add themselves to the waitlist and plan to attend. Due to limited supplies, wait-listed teens might not receive a Lock-In favor bag, however they will still be able to participate in Lock-In activities.

title: America250 Family Story Time — with Major Shane Sorensen
description:
In celebration of America250, come join us for a special family story time with guest, Major Shane Sorensen!

Major Shane Sorensen is a dedicated leader with 28 years of service in the Utah Army National Guard, currently serving as the Executive Officer at the Utah Training Center at Camp Williams. He manages the daily operations, administration, and logistical support for the installation. A combat-tested veteran, he has deployed twice in defense of the nation, serving in Iraq in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom and in Afghanistan in support of Operation Enduring Freedom. MAJ Sorensen enjoys spending his free time fishing, camping, and unwinding with a good action movie. He is married to Tiffany Sorensen and has two married children and two grandchildren. MAJ Sorensen loves his country and is extremely grateful for the freedom we all enjoy because of the sacrifice of so many in defense of liberty.

This class is sponsored by the Utah Historical Society.

title: Finding Alice — Artists Exploring Wonderland featuring Abelardo Morell
location: Provo Library — The Nelson Attic - Exhibit Space
description:
When Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland came out in 1865, it was a blockbuster success and was widely credited with changing the landscape of children’s literature, adding nonsensical fun to what had been a genre obsessed with moralizing. Since its first publication, it has been translated into over 175 languages and continues to inspire artists from around the world to interpret Carroll’s story in their own visionary ways.

Finding Alice: Artists Exploring Wonderland featuring Abelardo Morell features works from two photographic series by the acclaimed artist Abelardo Morell, as well as several versions of the book to examine how different artists have illustrated the classic story. Artists include Andrea D’Aquino (American b. 1979), Salvador Dalí (Spanish 1904–1989), Camille Rose Garcia (American b. 1970), Yayoi Kusama (Japanese b. 1929), Oleg Lipchenko (Ukrainian/Canadian b. 1957), Peter Newell (American 1862–1924), and Evgeny Alexandrovich Shukaev (Russian 1932–1988) among others.

Of his initial Alice in Wonderland series, Morell says, “I designed my images to be situated within a landscape made of books because it struck me that Carroll had linked Wonderland to the idea of discovering imagination by digging deep into the pages of a book. At this time my daughter, Laura, was seven years old and these pictures felt in part to be tributes to her, who like Alice, was an equally brave girl in my life.” Later, his experience during the COVID-19 pandemic and sheltering in place “sent [him] down another, different sort of rabbit hole. Suddenly, Alice’s adventures seemed to have a lot in common with what was going on in the world—and within me. His Through the Looking Glass series revolves around Alice stepping into a mirror, on the other side of which there is a topsy-turvy, unfamiliar, and illogical world. “What she encounters there seemed to me to have parallels to new realities in our present moment. Notably, however, in both her trips to Wonderland, Alice is resilient. She confronts the many disturbing things she encounters with determination and, in the end, she manages to adapt to her new situation. Alice’s rolling with the punches supplied me with an instructive guide to living in turbulent times. Brave Alice learns to deal with the irrational without ignoring it.  She makes her own sense out of nonsense.”

This exhibition was inspired by an exhibition of the same title, organized by the Ellen Noël Art Museum (Odessa, Texas) who has generously donated the books included in the exhibition, and provided curatorial support as the touring exhibition concept developed.

About the Artist, Abelardo Morell

Abelardo Morell and his family fled Cuba in 1962, moving to New York City. He is well known in the fine art and photographic communities for creating camera obscura images in various places around the world. In 1998, he was an artist-in-residence at Boston’s Gardner Museum, and the following year, Boston’s Museum of Fine Arts hosted his retrospective Abelardo Morell and the Camera Eye. A later retrospective entitled Abelardo Morell: The Universe Next Door was held at the Art Institute of Chicago in 2013, and was subsequently shown at the Getty Center in Los Angeles. The artist was also the subject of a documentary film, Shadow of the House, in 2007.

Abelardo Morell was awarded the CINTAS Foundation fellowship (1992); the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation Fellowship (1993); the International Center of Photography’s Infinity Award (2011); and the Lucie Awards Honoree for Achievement in Fine Art (2017). His work is in numerous private and public collections, including the Art Institute of Chicago; the Fondation Cartier, Paris; the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; Victoria & Albert Museum, London; and the Museum of Modern Art, New York. There are numerous publications and monographs on his work, including his illustration of Alice in Wonderland and Book of Books, with an introduction by author Nicholson Baker.

Abelardo Morell lives and works in Boston. He studied at Bowdoin College and holds an MFA from Yale University, and an honorary doctorate from Bowdoin. Until 2009, he was a professor of photography at Massachusetts College of Art. He is exclusively represented by the Edwynn Houk Gallery, New York.

description:
When Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland came out in 1865, it was a blockbuster success and was widely credited with changing the landscape of children’s literature, adding nonsensical fun to what had been a genre obsessed with moralizing. Since its first publication, it has been translated into over 175 languages and continues to inspire artists from around the world to interpret Carroll’s story in their own visionary ways.

Finding Alice: Artists Exploring Wonderland featuring Abelardo Morell features works from two photographic series by the acclaimed artist Abelardo Morell, as well as several versions of the book to examine how different artists have illustrated the classic story. Artists include Andrea D’Aquino (American b. 1979), Salvador Dalí (Spanish 1904–1989), Camille Rose Garcia (American b. 1970), Yayoi Kusama (Japanese b. 1929), Oleg Lipchenko (Ukrainian/Canadian b. 1957), Peter Newell (American 1862–1924), and Evgeny Alexandrovich Shukaev (Russian 1932–1988) among others.

Of his initial Alice in Wonderland series, Morell says, “I designed my images to be situated within a landscape made of books because it struck me that Carroll had linked Wonderland to the idea of discovering imagination by digging deep into the pages of a book. At this time my daughter, Laura, was seven years old and these pictures felt in part to be tributes to her, who like Alice, was an equally brave girl in my life.” Later, his experience during the COVID-19 pandemic and sheltering in place “sent [him] down another, different sort of rabbit hole. Suddenly, Alice’s adventures seemed to have a lot in common with what was going on in the world—and within me. His Through the Looking Glass series revolves around Alice stepping into a mirror, on the other side of which there is a topsy-turvy, unfamiliar, and illogical world. “What she encounters there seemed to me to have parallels to new realities in our present moment. Notably, however, in both her trips to Wonderland, Alice is resilient. She confronts the many disturbing things she encounters with determination and, in the end, she manages to adapt to her new situation. Alice’s rolling with the punches supplied me with an instructive guide to living in turbulent times. Brave Alice learns to deal with the irrational without ignoring it.  She makes her own sense out of nonsense.”

This exhibition was inspired by an exhibition of the same title, organized by the Ellen Noël Art Museum (Odessa, Texas) who has generously donated the books included in the exhibition, and provided curatorial support as the touring exhibition concept developed.

About the Artist, Abelardo Morell

Abelardo Morell and his family fled Cuba in 1962, moving to New York City. He is well known in the fine art and photographic communities for creating camera obscura images in various places around the world. In 1998, he was an artist-in-residence at Boston’s Gardner Museum, and the following year, Boston’s Museum of Fine Arts hosted his retrospective Abelardo Morell and the Camera Eye. A later retrospective entitled Abelardo Morell: The Universe Next Door was held at the Art Institute of Chicago in 2013, and was subsequently shown at the Getty Center in Los Angeles. The artist was also the subject of a documentary film, Shadow of the House, in 2007.

Abelardo Morell was awarded the CINTAS Foundation fellowship (1992); the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation Fellowship (1993); the International Center of Photography’s Infinity Award (2011); and the Lucie Awards Honoree for Achievement in Fine Art (2017). His work is in numerous private and public collections, including the Art Institute of Chicago; the Fondation Cartier, Paris; the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; Victoria & Albert Museum, London; and the Museum of Modern Art, New York. There are numerous publications and monographs on his work, including his illustration of Alice in Wonderland and Book of Books, with an introduction by author Nicholson Baker.

Abelardo Morell lives and works in Boston. He studied at Bowdoin College and holds an MFA from Yale University, and an honorary doctorate from Bowdoin. Until 2009, he was a professor of photography at Massachusetts College of Art. He is exclusively represented by the Edwynn Houk Gallery, New York.

title: Finding Alice — Artists Exploring Wonderland featuring Abelardo Morell
location: Provo Library — The Nelson Attic - Exhibit Space
description:

Finding Alice: Artists Exploring Wonderland featuring Abelardo Morell features works from two photographic series by the acclaimed artist Abelardo Morell, as well as several versions of the book to examine how different artists have illustrated the classic story. Artists include Andrea D’Aquino (American b. 1979), Salvador Dalí (Spanish 1904–1989), Camille Rose Garcia (American b. 1970), Yayoi Kusama (Japanese b. 1929), Oleg Lipchenko (Ukrainian/Canadian b. 1957), Peter Newell (American 1862–1924), and Evgeny Alexandrovich Shukaev (Russian 1932–1988) among others.

Of his initial Alice in Wonderland series, Morell says, “I designed my images to be situated within a landscape made of books because it struck me that Carroll had linked Wonderland to the idea of discovering imagination by digging deep into the pages of a book. At this time my daughter, Laura, was seven years old and these pictures felt in part to be tributes to her, who like Alice, was an equally brave girl in my life.” Later, his experience during the COVID-19 pandemic and sheltering in place “sent [him] down another, different sort of rabbit hole. Suddenly, Alice’s adventures seemed to have a lot in common with what was going on in the world—and within me. His Through the Looking Glass series revolves around Alice stepping into a mirror, on the other side of which there is a topsy-turvy, unfamiliar, and illogical world. “What she encounters there seemed to me to have parallels to new realities in our present moment. Notably, however, in both her trips to Wonderland, Alice is resilient. She confronts the many disturbing things she encounters with determination and, in the end, she manages to adapt to her new situation. Alice’s rolling with the punches supplied me with an instructive guide to living in turbulent times. Brave Alice learns to deal with the irrational without ignoring it.  She makes her own sense out of nonsense.”

This exhibition was inspired by an exhibition of the same title, organized by the Ellen Noël Art Museum (Odessa, Texas) who has generously donated the books included in the exhibition, and provided curatorial support as the touring exhibition concept developed.

Abelardo Morell and his family fled Cuba in 1962, moving to New York City. His work is in numerous private and public collections, including the Art Institute of Chicago; the Fondation Cartier, Paris; the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; Victoria & Albert Museum, London; and the Museum of Modern Art, New York. title: Finding Alice — Artists Exploring Wonderland featuring Abelardo Morell
location: Provo Library — The Nelson Attic - Exhibit Space
description:
When Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland came out in 1865, it was a blockbuster success and was widely credited with changing the landscape of children’s literature, adding nonsensical fun to what had been a genre obsessed with moralizing. Since its first publication, it has been translated into over 175 languages and continues to inspire artists from around the world to interpret Carroll’s story in their own visionary ways.

Finding Alice: Artists Exploring Wonderland featuring Abelardo Morell features works from two photographic series by the acclaimed artist Abelardo Morell, as well as several versions of the book to examine how different artists have illustrated the classic story. Artists include Andrea D’Aquino (American b. 1979), Salvador Dalí (Spanish 1904–1989), Camille Rose Garcia (American b. 1970), Yayoi Kusama (Japanese b. 1929), Oleg Lipchenko (Ukrainian/Canadian b. 1957), Peter Newell (American 1862–1924), and Evgeny Alexandrovich Shukaev (Russian 1932–1988) among others.

Of his initial Alice in Wonderland series, Morell says, “I designed my images to be situated within a landscape made of books because it struck me that Carroll had linked Wonderland to the idea of discovering imagination by digging deep into the pages of a book. At this time my daughter, Laura, was seven years old and these pictures felt in part to be tributes to her, who like Alice, was an equally brave girl in my life.” Later, his experience during the COVID-19 pandemic and sheltering in place “sent [him] down another, different sort of rabbit hole. Suddenly, Alice’s adventures seemed to have a lot in common with what was going on in the world—and within me. His Through the Looking Glass series revolves around Alice stepping into a mirror, on the other side of which there is a topsy-turvy, unfamiliar, and illogical world. “What she encounters there seemed to me to have parallels to new realities in our present moment. Notably, however, in both her trips to Wonderland, Alice is resilient. She confronts the many disturbing things she encounters with determination and, in the end, she manages to adapt to her new situation. Alice’s rolling with the punches supplied me with an instructive guide to living in turbulent times. Brave Alice learns to deal with the irrational without ignoring it.  She makes her own sense out of nonsense.”

This exhibition was inspired by an exhibition of the same title, organized by the Ellen Noël Art Museum (Odessa, Texas) who has generously donated the books included in the exhibition, and provided curatorial support as the touring exhibition concept developed.

About the Artist, Abelardo Morell

Abelardo Morell and his family fled Cuba in 1962, moving to New York City. He is well known in the fine art and photographic communities for creating camera obscura images in various places around the world. In 1998, he was an artist-in-residence at Boston’s Gardner Museum, and the following year, Boston’s Museum of Fine Arts hosted his retrospective Abelardo Morell and the Camera Eye. A later retrospective entitled Abelardo Morell: The Universe Next Door was held at the Art Institute of Chicago in 2013, and was subsequently shown at the Getty Center in Los Angeles. The artist was also the subject of a documentary film, Shadow of the House, in 2007.

Abelardo Morell was awarded the CINTAS Foundation fellowship (1992); the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation Fellowship (1993); the International Center of Photography’s Infinity Award (2011); and the Lucie Awards Honoree for Achievement in Fine Art (2017). His work is in numerous private and public collections, including the Art Institute of Chicago; the Fondation Cartier, Paris; the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; Victoria & Albert Museum, London; and the Museum of Modern Art, New York. There are numerous publications and monographs on his work, including his illustration of Alice in Wonderland and Book of Books, with an introduction by author Nicholson Baker.

Abelardo Morell lives and works in Boston. He studied at Bowdoin College and holds an MFA from Yale University, and an honorary doctorate from Bowdoin. Until 2009, he was a professor of photography at Massachusetts College of Art. He is exclusively represented by the Edwynn Houk Gallery, New York.

title: Utah Valley Operafest: — The Daughter of the Regiment
description:
About The Daughter of the Regiment
A comic opera by Gaetano Donizetti that follows Marie, a spirited young woman who was found as an orphaned baby and lovingly raised by an army regiment as their adopted daughter. She falls in love with Tonio, a local young man, but their happiness is threatened when Marie is claimed by an aristocratic relative who insists she leave her military family behind, learn the manners of high society, and marry a nobleman instead. As hidden truths about Marie's birth come to light, she must choose between social expectations and the people she loves.

This opera will be performed in French, but English subtitles will be projected during the performance.

About Utah Valley Operafest

Featuring an outstanding cast led by Grammy Award Winning tenor, Thomas Glenn as Tonio, Miriam Costa-Jackson as Marie, Christopher Holmes as Sulpice, and Demaree Brown as the Marquise of Berkenfeld, the production also showcases a lively ensemble of reform school boys—Jamen Zohner, Henry Curtis, Spencer Fidler, and Jude Swan. Adding even more excitement, the chorus is made up of talented young singers who are winners of Utah Valley Operafest's Future of Opera Vocal Competition, highlighting the next generation of rising operatic stars.

description:
Many Christmases ago, Charles Dickens would perform a one-man telling of his classic holiday tale, doing all the voices himself. Join us this holiday season as Bryan Johnson recreates that experience using Dickens’s original script.

Questions & Answers about this program: 

Q: I see that this says recommended for ages 8 and up. Do you mean it?

A: We mean our recommendation quite seriously. This is not a full-scale production of A Christmas Carol; think one-man show, not play. Our actor is fantastic, and we love this tradition, but our experience has been that sometimes, four-year-olds don't have the patience to make it through this performance.  

We are not asking for ages at the door, but if you have children who struggle sitting still and listening, we'd suggest that you attend a different holiday program. 

 Q: If registration fills up, can I come anyway?

A: Typically, not every single person who signs up for a ticket actually comes. We will have a standby line available for those who can't get tickets.
